report.answer: Mature registries mostly pull a listing or mark a version unselectable (npm unpublish/deprecate/security-holder, PyPI yank, crates.io yank, JetBrains hide). That half does not mutate an already-installed tree: 'nothing happens' on disk until the user updates, which is a valid and important finding (event-stream: npm removed registry objects and asked users to update). The forgotten half is a SEPARATE client channel: VS Code's malware block list auto-uninstalls, and Chrome Safe Browsing disables malicious installed extensions. Designing a prompt-payload marketplace after npm yank alone will miss already-installed clients unless a client-side check is specified.

cited_incident.name: npm event-stream / flatmap-stream (2018)
cited_incident.what_installed_users_experienced: Already-installed copies were not remotely wiped. npm told users to run npm audit and update to a later event-stream. Copay versions 5.0.2–5.1.0 shipped the malicious build; BitPay told those users not to run the app. Live 2026 registry: flatmap-stream is a security holding package (0.0.1-security); event-stream@3.3.6 is gone from versions but timestamped in time.
cited_incident.what_registry_did: Removed flatmap-stream and event-stream@3.3.6 from the npm Registry and took ownership of event-stream.

claims.claim: npm's publisher tools are unpublish and deprecate, not yank. Already-installed trees are not remotely deleted; deprecation warns on next install so 'builds will not break'.
claims.strongest_caveat: Security-holder replacement changes what a NEW install receives for a taken name; that is still not an uninstall of unpacked files.

claims.claim: PyPI yank is a resolver signal (simple API yanked field / data-yanked). A mechanical reinstall of a previously selected yanked file acts as if it had not been yanked.
claims.strongest_caveat: This run observed yanked=reason-string (not boolean true) on urllib3 files; PEP 691 treats a truthy yanked value as yanked.

claims.claim: crates.io yank marks the version yanked in the API, does not delete crate bytes, and does not break existing lockfiles or direct downloads.
claims.strongest_caveat: futures 0.2.0 is one yanked version, not a proof that every crate follows the same UI copy; the Cargo book states the rule.

claims.claim: VS Code's malware block list automatically uninstalls already-installed copies. Gallery deprecation/unpublish is a different channel: the live Material Theme listing is still public and carries no revoked field.
claims.strongest_caveat: The live gallery query is not itself a currently-blocked malware sample; it shows the listing channel. Auto-uninstall is quoted from vscode-docs Block List, not observed on this worktree's IDE.

claims.claim: JetBrains Marketplace hide-version does not affect users who already installed that version. The plugin JSON has isHidden and isBlocked fields.
claims.strongest_caveat: The live plugin 631 record is not hidden; it is used to show the field exists, not as a hidden-state sample.

claims.claim: Chrome reaches already-installed malicious/unsafe extensions by disabling them in the browser (Safe Browsing / 'Extensions Disabled'). That is a client channel, not CWS unpublish.
claims.strongest_caveat: Both Chrome rails are Google support pages (no public CWS item JSON). Same organisation; different properties (support.google.com/chrome vs /chrome_webstore). Graded E1 on the disable statement, not on a live malware-extension probe.

claims.claim: Cited incident: 2018 event-stream / flatmap-stream. npm removed flatmap-stream and event-stream@3.3.6 from the registry and told users to run npm audit and update. Already-installed users were not remotely cleaned; user action was required. Live registry still shows the security-holder name and a 3.3.6 time tombstone.
claims.strongest_caveat: The npm blog and Snyk postmortem share the same incident; they are independent publishers. The structured rail is today's registry JSON, not a 2018 packet capture.

report.question: When a published package must be pulled, what does each mature registry actually do (yank, unpublish, deprecate, advisory) and what does an ALREADY-INSTALLED client see - the half of revocation that most designs forget?

revocation_table.installed_client: Nothing is pushed to an already-extracted node_modules tree. A later install of a malware-replaced name receives the security holding package (flatmap-stream latest='0.0.1-security', description='security holding package'). event-stream@3.3.6 is absent from versions (installable=False) but remains in the time tombstone (2018-09-09T08:28:59.503Z). Deprecation warns at next install; it does not uninstall.
revocation_table.registry_action: unpublish (72h / low-traffic criteria) or deprecate; security-holder replacement for malware names
revocation_table.strongest_caveat: npm Security can replace the registry document (security-holder) so NEW installs change; that is not the same as mutating disks that already unpacked the old tarball.

revocation_table.installed_client: An already-installed distribution is not uninstalled. PEP 592: a computer mechanically reinstalling a previously selected yanked file 'acts as if it had not been yanked'. Live simple API: 8 yanked urllib3 files, e.g. urllib3-1.25-py2.py3-none-any.whl yanked='Broken release'.
revocation_table.registry_action: yank (PEP 592 data-yanked / JSON yanked) plus limited delete
revocation_table.strongest_caveat: Installers SHOULD warn when they do install a yanked file; a lockfile pin can still fetch it.

revocation_table.installed_client: futures 0.2.0 has yanked=True on the crates.io API and still advertises a download path. Cargo: yanking 'does not delete any data'; 'Existing lock files or direct downloads are not affected'.
revocation_table.registry_action: yank (no user deletion of crate bytes)
revocation_table.strongest_caveat: A fresh checkout without a lockfile will not newly depend on the yanked version; that is resolver policy, not an installed-tree wipe.

revocation_table.installed_client: Two channels. (1) Gallery: live query for equinusocio.vsc-material-theme returns displayName='Material Theme — Deprecated' flags='validated, public'; no revoked/blocked field is present, so listing deprecation is not a kill-switch in this JSON. (2) Malware block list (vscode-docs): a verified malicious extension is removed from the Marketplace AND 'automatically uninstalled by VS Code' on already-installed instances.
revocation_table.registry_action: gallery unpublish/deprecate PLUS a separate malware block list
revocation_table.strongest_caveat: Do not treat gallery unpublish/deprecate as the installed-client story. Auto-uninstall is documented only for the malware block list.

revocation_table.installed_client: Official hide-version docs: 'This won’t affect users who have already installed this version, but new users won't be able to download it unless you provide the direct link'. API for plugin 631 Python exposes isHidden=False isBlocked=False (fields exist; this plugin is not hidden).
revocation_table.registry_action: hide version / unpublish or remove after review
revocation_table.strongest_caveat: Post-approval unpublish is documented as a marketplace listing action; the hide-version page is the explicit installed-client negative. Manual uninstall remains user-initiated.

revocation_table.installed_client: Mere CWS unpublish is not the kill-switch for consumer Chrome (enterprise ExtensionUnpublishedAvailability defaults to allowing unpublished extensions). The installed-client path is Chrome itself: Safe Browsing help states 'If you have an abusive or malicious extension installed, Chrome disables it.' CWS help: Chrome turns off extensions that 'didn't come from the Chrome Web Store or were determined unsafe'.
revocation_table.registry_action: unpublish from CWS; malware/unsafe handled by Chrome client
revocation_table.strongest_caveat: Chrome has no public package JSON analogous to npm/PyPI. The API rail here is Google's Safe Browsing product contract, not a CWS item document. Same publisher as the CWS help page; different product surface.
